 Want to challenge against the best: Kyle Jamieson on Virat Kohli, Sooryavanshi’s Rise, KL Rahul, and Tests
 Kyle Jamieson delves deeper on how the bowlers are trying to adjust to the demands of modern-day limited-overs cricket. The pacer also shared his thoughts on Vaibhav, Kohli and Rohit. By Subhayan Chakraborty October 28, 2026 Updated: October 28, 2026 No Comments 6 Mins Read

 Subhayan Chakraborty, Wellington 
 There is a quiet pragmatic lucidity with which Kyle Jamieson dissects modern cricket. Towering over conversations with the same imposing stillness he brings to the top of his bowling mark, the New Zealand all-rounder does not deal in breathless hype or dramatic fatalism. Facing a packed touring Indian side across formats, Jamieson views the contest through the lens of calculated attrition, tactical evolution, and pure competitive relish.
 “It’s obviously such a marquee sort of tour, and obviously within that you’ve got the different series and different formats to look forward to,” Jamieson reflected during a select media interaction in Wellington. The Kiwi all-rounder will be next seen in Black Caps’ colours in the ODI format, skipping the last two T20Is against India. “ODIs will be great,” he said. “We’ve obviously had some great tussles over the years, and yeah, I’m sure this one will be no different.”
 The bilateral rivalry has long offered gripping theatre, but this stretch carries an extra layer of emotion with the presence of Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli, marking their final competitive outing on New Zealand soil. While the prospect will stir sentiments across the cricketing fraternity, Jamieson sees it as a celebratory occasion for spectators, alongside a stern personal test.
 “I just think it’s great for the fans, right?” he smiled. “Probably the last chance to see them on home soil, and for those of us that get to share the field with them, it’s always special no matter the team or the part of the world that you’re playing in. So, no different this time, but yeah, it’d be nice to go toe-to-toe again on home soil.”
 Asked whether Kohli’s rich vein of form could carry him toward an elusive century of international tons in the next 12 months or so, Jamieson joked, “Well, I don’t think he can get here on this tour, so that’s… don’t have to worry about too much.” However, there’s an unreserved admiration for his former RCB team mate. “He could probably just go on and on,” Jamieson noted. “In terms of where his skill level is and where his physical body is at, you could probably keep playing for a number of years. When you get sort of world-class talent, right, they don’t ever sort of lose it. As long as he’s putting on an Indian shirt or an RCB shirt or whoever’s shirt he’s putting on, I’m sure he’ll be right at the top of his game.”
 With the teenage phenomenon Vaibhav Sooryavanshi having captured the global imagination, Jamieson acknowledged the staggering evolution of the sport. “He’s a serious player, right? We talk about the age, which is obviously so impressive, but it’s world-class for any age,” Jamieson said. “For us, the idea of walking onto an international field at 15 is just not something that’s ever done. Very impressive… and it’ll be just cool to watch as a spectator over the next 10, 15, 20 years, however long he plays for, and see what that career arc looks like.”
 With boundaries shrinking and willow dominating leather, fast bowlers are perpetually searching for oxygen in shorter formats of the game. “Still trying to work it out (on how to tackle this), I think,” he admitted with candid self-awareness. “The game’s leaning towards the batters a lot more. The wickets are certainly batter-friendly, boundaries are small. So, I guess it’s up to us as bowlers to try and find ways to combat it, and I’m not sure too many guys have sort of figured it out just yet, but that’s kind of the challenge that’s in front of us.”
 That harsh reality makes the transition to red-ball cricket a welcome prospect for quicks, with New Zealand set to face India in a two-Test series after five ODIs. “It’s nice to get a little bit more back in our favour with the red ball in general,” Jamieson noted. “The wickets tend to have a little bit more life in them, a little bit more pace and bounce, a little bit more grass coverage, so it tends to support seam bowling a lot more than probably what the white-ball wickets do. The trend over the last sort of five or six years, it tends to be more seam-bowler friendly, which hopefully holds.”
 That assistance will be vital as both teams eye crucial World Test Championship stakes. Jamieson first broke through against India during the 2020 home series and later starred in the inaugural WTC final, cementing an enviable record against them. “You sort of know when you’re playing India, you have to be right at the top of your game,” he asserted. “Whenever you’re faced with that challenge as a player, it’s sort of what you want to walk towards. You want to challenge yourself against the best. You know that you’re going to need your best to even just be competitive. Some great memories from when I first started out and had some good tussles over the last sort of five, six years, and I’m sure this series will be no different.”
 Among the sternest obstacles standing in their way is KL Rahul, an experienced campaigner, well-versed in countering unfamiliar conditions abroad. Despite Rahul’s low score in the recent India A outing, Jamieson refused to discount his Delhi Capitals teammate. “He’s obviously world-class, right? And he’s done it all around the world, especially in conditions that are kind of similar to here,” Jamieson pointed out. “I wouldn’t really read too much into how that first sort of game (India A) went. Know his quality, and have shared a few net sessions earlier in the year through the IPL. So we’ve certainly seen a lot of each other, and it will be interesting to see who comes out on top.”
 Navigating such high-stakes assignments alongside the impending four-Test tour of Australia requires meticulous planning. Opting to skip the remaining two T20Is to turn out for Canterbury in the domestic Ford Trophy, Jamieson explained the logic driving his workload management. “Quite a unique summer in terms of this full tour with India, and then into the four Tests in Australia as well,” he concluded. “Trying to just zoom out a little bit and go, ‘How do we best manage things?’ Good chance to sort of tap out, play a Ford Trophy game, a little bit more time on feet, get a few more overs, a few more spells than you can in T20s… felt like the right fit for me leading into the one-days and the Tests.”
